openingProblem.problem: In 1947 Kennan proposed a 'patient' policy of containment. By 1965 the US was bombing North Vietnam. How did a policy of patience become a policy of war, and what did the Soviet idea of 'peaceful co-existence' change?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did containment change in its aims or only in its methods?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Containment defined and militarised, 1947–1953
chunks.body:
**Containment** was the basic American strategy of the Cold War. Its author, the diplomat George Kennan, wrote in his anonymous "X-Article" of 1947 that US policy must be "a long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies". Soviet pressure was to be met by "counter-force at a series of constantly shifting geographical and political points". Kennan predicted that, held in check, Soviet power would eventually either break up or "mellow".

What did containment mean in practice? From the start it was disputed. The columnist Walter Lippmann attacked Kennan for failing to separate vital interests from peripheral ones, as if the US must resist everywhere. In fact Kennan wanted above all to protect the world's great industrial centres (Western Europe, Japan and the US) and saw the Soviet threat as mainly political, to be met with economic aid such as the Marshall Plan and with propaganda and covert action. His successor at the State Department, Paul Nitze, saw the threat in military terms.

Nitze won. In April 1950, shaken by the Communist victory in China and the first Soviet atomic test, his team completed **NSC-68**. It described a Soviet Union "animated by a new fanatic faith" and called for a massive build-up of conventional and nuclear arms. It also widened containment to the whole globe: "a defeat of free institutions anywhere is a defeat everywhere." Kennan and others objected that the US already had a large military lead, but the North Korean invasion of South Korea in June 1950 settled the argument. Between 1950 and 1953 US defence spending almost tripled as a share of national output, from 5 to 14.2 per cent.

Under Eisenhower, containment rested heavily on nuclear threat. NATO's doctrine of "massive retaliation" promised a large-scale American nuclear response to an attack on any member. John Foster Dulles had called in 1952 for the "rollback" of Soviet power and the "liberation" of Eastern Europe, but no administration acted on it.

This mattered because containment changed from a mainly political and economic strategy into a global military one, which meant that after 1950 any Communist advance anywhere could be treated as a threat to the United States.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Kennan's containment was limited and mainly political.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Lippmann thought the X-Article implied resisting everywhere.
It only became policy because of the Korean War.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Containment remained the core strategy throughout.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Dulles's 'rollback' showed pressure for a more aggressive line.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was NSC-68 a turning point in the policy of containment between 1947 and 1953?
Compare and contrast containment in Europe and in Asia between 1947 and 1975.

useItInAnEssay.claim: NSC-68 was a turning point because it turned containment from a selective, mainly economic strategy into a global military one.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Kennan had favoured economic aid to protect key industrial centres, but NSC-68 called for a massive arms build-up and declared that 'a defeat of free institutions anywhere is a defeat everywhere'.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the US now treated every Communist advance as a threat, so defence spending almost tripled as a share of GDP between 1950 and 1953.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, NSC-68 became policy only because North Korea invaded the South in June 1950, so events rather than the document made the change.
useItInAnEssay.judge: NSC-68 was therefore the blueprint of the turning point, and Korea its trigger.

chunks.title: Peaceful co-existence and its limits, 1953–1960
chunks.body:
Stalin's death in 1953 opened the door to change. His successor as Premier, Georgi Malenkov, made the first overtures to the West, a "peace offensive". By 1955 **Nikita Khrushchev** had emerged as sole leader. In his "secret speech" to the Twentieth Party Congress in February 1956 he denounced Stalin's crimes and, in foreign policy, abandoned Stalin's assumption that war with the capitalist West was inevitable. In its place he advocated **peaceful co-existence**: competition between the systems without war.

Peaceful co-existence had clear limits. The Soviet bloc was formalised as a military alliance: the **Warsaw Pact** was founded on 14 May 1955, days after West Germany joined NATO, and the USSR used it to keep its satellites in line. When Khrushchev's speech encouraged demands for reform in Eastern Europe, Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising of 1956, at the cost of thousands of casualties. The Eisenhower administration watched but did not intervene; "rollback" proved to be a slogan.

The arms race continued too. At Geneva in 1955 Eisenhower proposed "open skies" mutual aerial inspection; Khrushchev refused. On 4 October 1957 the USSR launched **Sputnik**, the first artificial satellite, and in the same year tested the first intercontinental ballistic missile. Americans feared they had fallen behind, the arms and space races accelerated, and Kennedy later campaigned on a supposed "missile gap".

Yet there were early signs of détente in the late 1950s, and a summit was planned in Paris for May 1960. On 1 May an American U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union. Eisenhower refused to apologise and admitted the programme; the Soviet delegation left Paris as the summit was about to begin. Khrushchev, publicly committed to peaceful co-existence, gave up on Eisenhower and waited for his successor.

This mattered because peaceful co-existence changed the language of Soviet policy without ending the rivalry, which meant that relaxation and confrontation alternated: Geneva and détente on the one hand, Hungary, Sputnik and the U-2 on the other.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Khrushchev's peaceful co-existence was a real change from Stalin's view of inevitable war.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It did not stop Soviet repression in Hungary.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet control of Eastern Europe remained non-negotiable.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The West, too, accepted it by not intervening.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The arms race and espionage limited co-existence.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both sides still sought summits and arms control.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that peaceful co-existence was a propaganda slogan rather than a real change in Soviet policy with reference to the period 1956 to 1962.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Peaceful co-existence was a real change in Soviet doctrine, but it did not change Soviet behaviour in its own sphere.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In February 1956 Khrushchev abandoned Stalin's belief that war with the West was inevitable, yet later that year Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that co-existence applied to relations with the West but not to the satellites, so the USSR could seek détente while holding its bloc by force.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Khrushchev's pursuit of a summit in 1960 shows the change was more than propaganda, since the U-2 incident, not Soviet policy, wrecked it.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Peaceful co-existence was therefore a genuine but limited change.

chunks.title: Containment in Asia and the Middle East, 1950–1968
chunks.body:
After 1950 containment became global. In Asia it meant drawing lines around Communist China. When the Korean War began in June 1950, the US sent its Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait, protecting Chiang Kai-shek's government on Taiwan. In 1954 the US led the creation of the **Southeast Asia Treaty Organization** (SEATO). When the People's Republic bombarded the offshore islands of Jinmen and Mazu from September 1954, Washington signed a Mutual Defense Treaty with Taiwan, and in January 1955 Congress gave Eisenhower authority to defend Taiwan and the islands. The administration considered options up to nuclear weapons before Beijing offered talks. When the shelling resumed in 1958, the US re-supplied the island garrisons and the bombardment ended.

In the Middle East, the **Eisenhower Doctrine** of 1957 promised American aid, including troops, to any country threatened by "any nation controlled by international communism". Eisenhower feared that the decline of British and French prestige after the Suez Crisis had left a vacuum the Soviets might fill. In 1958 US troops landed in Lebanon.

The heaviest commitment was in **Vietnam**. In May 1954 the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu fell to Ho Chi Minh's forces after a four-month siege, and France withdrew from Indochina. The Geneva Conference divided Vietnam and called for elections to reunite it. The Communists seemed likely to win, so the US, citing SEATO, backed the South Vietnamese leader Ngo Dinh Diem when he refused to hold them. American officials also valued Southeast Asia as a market and source of raw materials for Japan. By 1959 a Communist insurgency had begun in the South. After reported attacks on US destroyers in August 1964 (doubts later arose about the second), Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, with only two senators voting against. In February 1965 the bombing campaign Operation Rolling Thunder began, and American ground troops followed.

This mattered because global containment drew the US into conflicts where the enemy was as much local nationalism as Soviet expansion, which meant that by the mid-1960s the strategy Kennan had designed for Europe was being tested in the jungles of Vietnam.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Containment in Asia meant defending Taiwan and building alliances.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The US was careful not to commit itself to defending every island.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Eisenhower Doctrine extended containment to the Middle East.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Lebanon intervention dealt with a local rivalry, not Soviet aggression.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Vietnam showed containment colliding with nationalism.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The US saw Vietnam as part of a global Communist threat.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Containment in Asia succeeded in protecting Taiwan but failed in Vietnam, because it misread nationalism as Soviet expansion.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The US defended Jinmen and Mazu in 1954–55 and 1958, but in Vietnam it backed Diem's refusal to hold elections the Communists seemed likely to win.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the US tied itself to an unpopular government, so the insurgency that began in 1959 drew it into a war it could not win.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, from Washington's point of view each step followed the logic of NSC-68, under which a defeat anywhere was a defeat everywhere.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Containment in Asia therefore worked where the US defended a stable ally and failed where it tried to create one.

chunks.title: Limits and adjustments, 1962–1979
chunks.body:
By the 1960s the costs of confrontation were clear. The rapid escalation of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962 pushed both superpowers to seek an agreement that could help them avoid nuclear destruction. The **Limited Test Ban Treaty** of 1963, signed by the US, the USSR and Britain, banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and underwater. It did little to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, but it set a precedent for the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 and SALT I in 1972. By the mid-1960s the two sides had reached approximate nuclear parity, and security rested on "mutually assured destruction": neither could strike first without being destroyed in return. Threatening nuclear war to win diplomatic advantage lost its credibility.

Vietnam exposed the limits of containment by force. When Richard Nixon took office in January 1969 he set out to end American involvement "honorably". He began withdrawing troops and building up South Vietnam's army ("Vietnamization"), while negotiating in secret and using heavy bombing to pressure Hanoi. He also sought to reshape the war's international setting by improving relations with Moscow and Beijing, giving them "bigger fish to fry" than support for North Vietnam. A peace agreement was signed on 27 January 1973 and American troops came home. But the war went on, and on 30 April 1975 North Vietnamese tanks rolled into the Presidential Palace in Saigon.

Did containment fail? In Vietnam, plainly. Yet the Office of the Historian concludes that every administration after Truman's, until the collapse of communism in 1989, adopted "a variation of Kennan's containment policy". The US never withdrew into isolation, but it never tried to roll back Soviet power either. What changed was the method: from the massive retaliation of the 1950s, through the war in Vietnam, to the arms control and détente of the 1970s.

This mattered because the failure in Vietnam pushed the US towards negotiation with its rivals, which meant that containment survived as a goal while détente became its new method.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Arms control reflected the dangers of nuclear parity.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Test Ban Treaty had little practical effect on proliferation.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Vietnam exposed the limits of military containment.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nixon's diplomacy with Moscow and Beijing kept containment's aims.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Containment survived as a goal while its methods changed.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Critics argued that détente was a retreat from containment.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that containment by direct military intervention gave way to containment by diplomacy, so negotiation with the Communist powers became part of US strategy.

useItInAnEssay.judge: Vietnam therefore ended containment by ground war but not containment itself.

arguments.claim: NSC-68's arms build-up and global scope (named factor first).
Kennan's original, limited containment.
Korea turns NSC-68 into policy.
Continuity: containment's basic aim survived.

modelPlan.counter: Lippmann argued that Kennan's X-Article was already open-ended, so the global scope was implicit from 1947.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did containment change in kind? Yes: from economic aid for key centres to a global arms build-up.

segments.text: NSC-68 was the blueprint of a turning point in containment.
Kennan had favoured economic aid to protect key industrial centres, but NSC-68 called for a massive arms build-up and declared that 'a defeat of free institutions anywhere is a defeat everywhere'.
This meant that containment became global and military, so defence spending rose from 5 to 14.2 per cent of GDP between 1950 and 1953.
However, Kennan and others opposed NSC-68, and only the North Korean invasion of June 1950 made its recommendations policy.
NSC-68 was therefore the turning point in ideas, and Korea the turning point in practice.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Peaceful co-existence was a propaganda slogan rather than a real change in Soviet policy.” Discuss with reference to the period 1956 to 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: propaganda, not real change
decodeKey.judgement: Whether Soviet doctrine and behaviour changed, and towards whom

modelPlan.thesis: Peaceful co-existence was a real change in Soviet doctrine towards the West, shown by Khrushchev's pursuit of summits, but it did not extend to the satellites or end the arms race, so the claim is only partly valid.

arguments.claim: Against the claim: rejection of inevitable war.
Against the claim: early détente and the planned summit.
For the claim: Hungary and the Warsaw Pact.
For the claim: the arms race and refusal of inspection.

modelPlan.counter: Khrushchev also boasted of Soviet missile superiority, using co-existence alongside pressure.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did Soviet behaviour towards the West change? Partly: summits were sought, but the arms race continued.

segments.text: Peaceful co-existence was a real change in Soviet doctrine, not merely propaganda.
In February 1956 Khrushchev abandoned Stalin's assumption that war with the West was inevitable, and in 1960 he prepared for a summit in Paris.
This meant that the USSR now sought to compete without war, so it was the U-2 incident, not Soviet policy, that wrecked the summit.
However, Soviet forces crushed Hungary in 1956 and Khrushchev refused 'open skies', so co-existence did not reach the satellites or the arms race.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: co-existence was real but limited.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the success of containment in Asia between 1950 and 1975.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: whether Communist control spread

modelPlan.thesis: Containment in Asia succeeded where the US defended a stable ally such as Taiwan, but failed in Vietnam, where it tied itself to an unpopular regime against a nationalist movement.

arguments.claim: Success: defending Taiwan, 1950–58.
Success: alliances such as SEATO.
Failure: Diem and the Geneva elections.
Failure: escalation and the fall of Saigon.

modelPlan.counter: By 1972 Nixon's diplomacy with Beijing and Moscow had achieved containment's aims by other means.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by whether Communist control spread, containment held in Taiwan but failed in Vietnam.

segments.text: Containment in Asia had mixed results: it held the line in Taiwan but failed in Vietnam.
The US defended Jinmen and Mazu in 1954–55 and 1958, but in Vietnam it backed Diem's refusal to hold elections, and Saigon fell on 30 April 1975.
This meant that US power could protect an established ally, but could not create a stable state where the Communists had stronger popular support.
However, the US kept its key Asian interests, such as Japan and Taiwan, which Kennan had seen as what mattered.
Containment in Asia therefore succeeded in its core and failed at its edges.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast containment in Europe and in Asia between 1947 and 1975.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: In both regions the US contained Communism through alliances and aid, but in Europe containment kept the rivalry cold, whereas in Asia it led to two hot wars, because there the opponent was Communist nationalism as well as Soviet power.

arguments.claim: Similarity: alliances in both regions.
Similarity: commitment to defend allies.
Difference: no war in Europe, war in Asia.
Difference: the nature of the opponent.

modelPlan.counter: Kennan's original containment focused on Europe and Japan, so Asian wars were an extension he opposed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? The nature of the opponent: nationalism in Vietnam made military containment fail.

segments.text: Containment used similar tools in Europe and Asia, but with very different results.
In Europe NATO and massive retaliation kept the rivalry cold, whereas in Asia the US fought in Korea and, from 1965, in Vietnam.
This meant that in Europe the US faced Soviet power across a stable line, while in Asia it faced Communist nationalists such as Ho Chi Minh.
However, in both regions the US built alliances and defended its allies, as NATO in Europe and the defence of Taiwan in 1958 show.
The decisive difference was therefore the opponent, which explains why containment held in Europe and failed in Vietnam.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the arms race between 1949 and 1963.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The arms race was driven by mutual fear of falling behind, sharpened by the Soviet bomb, NSC-68 and Sputnik; its consequences were espionage, crises and, after Cuba, the first arms control agreement.

arguments.claim: Cause: the Soviet bomb and NSC-68.
Cause: Sputnik and the missile gap.
Consequence: espionage and the U-2 crisis.
Consequence: the Limited Test Ban Treaty.

modelPlan.counter: The 'missile gap' was largely imaginary: Kennedy's administration found the balance still favoured the US.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? Arms control, which began with the Test Ban Treaty and led to SALT.

segments.text: The arms race was driven above all by mutual fear of falling behind.
After the Soviet bomb NSC-68 called for a massive build-up, and Sputnik in 1957 created fears of a 'missile gap'.
This meant that each side's progress drove the other to accelerate, so both turned to espionage, as the U-2 flights show.
However, the race also produced its own brake: after the Cuban crisis the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963 began arms control.
Fear therefore caused the arms race, and the danger it created led to the first steps to limit it.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of the Vietnam War on United States containment policy between 1964 and 1975.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The impact of the Vietnam War
decodeKey.judgement: How far Vietnam changed the methods and aims of containment

modelPlan.thesis: Vietnam forced the US to abandon containment by ground war and turn to Vietnamization, negotiation and diplomacy with Moscow and Beijing, though the goal of containing Communism remained.

arguments.claim: Escalation after Tonkin.
Vietnamization and withdrawal.
Diplomacy with Moscow and Beijing.
Containment's goal survived.

modelPlan.counter: The war's outcome in 1975 suggests the policy had failed rather than adapted.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did Vietnam change containment's aims or methods? Methods: the goal survived until 1989.

segments.text: Vietnam changed the methods of containment rather than its aims.
After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of August 1964 the US escalated, but from 1969 Nixon withdrew troops and sought better relations with Moscow and Beijing.
This meant that containment by ground war gave way to containment by diplomacy, so the 1972 summits became part of the strategy.
However, the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 showed that in Vietnam itself containment had failed.
Vietnam therefore transformed how the US contained Communism, not whether it did.
